title: Chapter 129 – The Sunken Lamp
html:
[Southern Desert – Lin Jian]

The city of Sunken Lamp is built around a hole.

Jian sees it first from the dunes, on the hundred and sixty-second day of the journey, in the thin white glare of noon: a low sprawl of yellow brick and awnings spread across the desert floor like a spill of grain, and at its center a great round pit, a thousand paces across, ringed with terraces and stairs. Dust devils walk across it. Birds wheel in the heat. Around the rim, set into the walls at every level, are thousands upon thousands of small clay lamps, each one cupped in a niche, none of them lit.

"They light them at dusk," says Tan Bo, from the box of the lead wagon, wiping his brow. "Every night. A hundred thousand wicks. The pilgrims come from the whole south to see it." He flicks the reins. "It is the only sight in the Kettle worth the journey. Also the only place where nobody asks questions about your cargo."

"Why is it called the Sunken Lamp?"

"Because of the story." Tan Bo shrugs. "There was once a great lamp at the bottom of the pit. Older than the city. Older than the road. It burned for a thousand years without oil. Then one night it went out, and the sand rose up, and the well filled in, and the people built their city around the place where the light used to be." He spits cheerfully over the side. "Nobody has seen it since. But it is a good story. The temple makes a lot of money from it."

Yue, on the wagon bed behind him, has not looked up from her ledger for an hour. Now she lifts her head, and her face, under the sun-bleached scarf, is very still.

"It is not a story," she says. "It is directly under us."

* * *

Tan Ruyan meets them at the Pilgrims' Gate with a ledger in one hand and a sword in the other.

She is thirty-six now, tall and spare, with a hard handsome face and a streak of white in her black hair. She wears the dark green of a Tan trade-master, with a silver chain across her chest, and a Foundation Establishment Peak's quiet, banked pressure like a hand on the air. Behind her stand twenty guards in good armor, and a clerk, and a boy holding an umbrella.

She looks at Jian for a long moment. Then she lowers the sword, and the ledger, and smiles.

"You are late," she says. "I heard in the spring."

"I took the long road."

"I heard that too. Fifty Salt Hands." She steps forward and clasps his forearm, hard. "My uncle's silver. I have been following it since you left the Sect. It leads to a counting-house in the eastern port, and from there to a man who keeps a blue crane on his seal and a plum-colored ledger in his safe." Her eyes are dark and hard. "He is dead now. I saw to it. But there will be others."

"I am sorry."

"Do not be. It was the first thing that has ever gone right in my family." She releases him, steps back, and looks at Yue, and at Pebble, who sits on the barrel with her head tilted, studying the new arrival. "This is the sister."

"Lin Yue," says Yue, bowing.

"The one who hears." Ruyan's mouth twitches. "I have heard of you. A girl with a book of doors. My clerks quote your ledger in the Hall." She bows back, shortly, more deeply than she needs to. "I will find you a bed. And a map. You will want a map."

"We have no need—"

"You have every need." Ruyan is already walking, her boots ringing on the flagstones. "The temple has a forbidden quarter. Nobody goes in. The priests say it holds the sleeping lamp. They have been saying so for three hundred years, and charging a silver for the privilege of not looking at it." She glances back. "I have a key."

* * *

The Tan house in Sunken Lamp has a courtyard with a dry fountain and a table laid for six, and Ruyan serves the meal herself, which Jian understands is an honor.

It is plain food: flatbread, lamb with dried apricots, a bowl of cold yogurt with mint. They eat in the dusk with the lamps of the great pit coming alight above the roofs, one by one, a slow wave of gold climbing the rim. Yue eats little. Pebble eats a good deal. Ruyan eats like a woman who has not had a proper meal in a year and does not intend to explain.

"My mother died last winter," she says abruptly, tearing bread. "Tan Mei. She paid the Registry seventeen years to keep me out of the family book, and on her deathbed she told me where the receipts were. It took me a month to read them." Her voice is flat. "I am the Tan trade-master now. The old men voted. Three of them did not live to see the count."

"I am sorry."

"You said that already." She pushes the plate away. "I do not want your sorrow. I want to know what you are doing in the south."

He tells her. Not everything. The Dock, the sister sites, the Operators who left no record. He leaves out the Cole door and the Chain and the name on the Roll. He tells her only that there are rooms under the world, and that he thinks someone left something in them for him.

She listens in silence, with her chin on her fist.

"I have a ledger of favors," she says at the end. "You gave me an Earthheart root, once, when we were nineteen. I did not forget it." She taps the table. "I will pay you in the one coin you cannot print. I will keep the door. Whatever is down there, whatever you find, nobody will go down that stair without passing me. I have twenty guards and a priest on my payroll, and the Nameless, if I can trust him, which I cannot."

"You do not have to."

"I do. That is the nature of a favor." She smiles, without warmth. "Besides. If the world is really made of doors, I would like to be the one holding the key."

Yue, across the table, has put down her bread.

"Ruyan," she says carefully. "Do you hear it?"

"Hear what?"

"The lamps." Yue's face is turned up to the rim of the pit, where the thousands of small clay flames have all begun, together, to flicker. "They are not burning in the wind. They are burning in time."

"In time with what?"

"With him." She does not point. She does not need to.

Jian looks down. In his breast pocket, wrapped in a handkerchief, the little wooden spoon is warm against his ribs. And in the pit, a hundred thousand wicks tremble, bright and gold, in the same slow rhythm as the hum behind his teeth.

* * *

That night, on a roof under the stars, he finds the hole.

He had expected it. Pebble had warned him, and so had the panel: Each step is remembered by the Door. He has walked through four seams since the Kettle, and in thirty-eight years he has not been so afraid of anything as of what he might discover. He lies on his back on the warm clay tiles with his hands behind his head and the whole desert sky blazing overhead, and he begins, carefully, to name the stars.

Hearth. Ladle. The Weaver's Girl. The Two Oxen. They come easily. He goes down the list of the winter ones. The Heron. The Lamp-bearer. Then the long river of lesser lights on the southern rim of the world.

He stops.

There is a star there. A bright one, orange, low on the horizon, with a smaller companion. He knows it. He has known it since he was a child; he can feel the shape of the word sitting at the back of his tongue, as familiar as his own hand. He opens his mouth.

Nothing.

He tries again. There is a gap. A smooth round absence, as if the word had been scooped out with a spoon. He knows that the star is bright. He knows it has a name. He knows he has said that name a thousand times, to Wenyuan, to Feng, to Kuang on the Gate stair on a night of heavy frost.

He does not know what it is.

He lies there for a long time. A wind comes up, soft and dry, and moves across the roof, smelling of dust and cold and distant rain. He thinks of the spoon. He thinks of the baby name he lost. He thinks, with the odd clear calm of a man adding a column of figures, that a Door which asks for a memory every time it opens, and has lately asked for none, has simply been keeping a ledger.

Memory cost: none yet.

"Four steps," he says quietly. "Four stars."

He does not know how he knows. But somewhere above him, in the long white river of the southern sky, a single orange light burns on, nameless and patient and entirely unmoved.

The forbidden quarter is a flight of sixty steps down the side of the pit, behind a screen of dead lamps.

It is evening when they reach it, the first lamps of the night just beginning to flicker in the walls above, a trembling garland of gold in the rising dusk. The air is cooling fast. Ruyan has bribed two priests and borrowed a lantern, and she leads them along a narrow ledge at the edge of the terraces, with the city lights spread out above them and the dark mouth of the pit opening below. Pebble rides on Yue's shoulder. Jian walks last.

He is aware, with every step, of the hum.

It is not the Cole door. It is something below it, deeper, a long flat tone like a note held on a great organ, so low that it is more felt than heard. It has been growing since they entered the city. It sits behind his teeth. It makes the soles of his feet tingle.

"There," says Yue.

She has stopped. The ledge ends at a blank wall of blackened brick, with a faded painting of a lamp. She puts out one small hand, flat, and lays it against the paint. Her eyes close.

"It is a door," she says. "Not a big one. The same shape as the Gate wall, but thin. Like a leaf. It was shut from the other side, and a long time ago." She opens her eyes and looks at Ruyan. "May I?"

"It is not my door," says Ruyan. "I only have the key."

"Then open it."

Ruyan draws a small iron key from her sleeve. It is rust-red and old, and there is no keyhole in the wall. She looks at it, and then at the painting, and laughs under her breath.

"I paid forty silver for this," she says, "and a promise of favors to four priests. I should like very much for it not to be a trick."

She presses the key to the painted lamp, at the wick. The wall sighs, like a held breath released, and swings inward on a dark and silent stair.

* * *

The Nameless is waiting at the top.

Jian had half hoped it would not follow them. It had trailed the caravan through the last hundred and sixty days, forty paces behind, never closing the distance, never lagging; it had walked into Sunken Lamp behind the last wagon and stopped at the Pilgrims' Gate when they did. Now it stands at the head of the forbidden stair with its hands at its sides, silent, a thin gray shape in the guttering lamplight, as though it had been waiting for them all along.

Ruyan has her sword half out of the sheath. "Who is that?"

"Nobody," says Jian. "He is following us."

"He is a Registry Number."

"He used to be."

"That is not a distinction." She does not lower the blade. "Lin Jian, I have bled a fortune to get this thing off my family. I will not have one standing at my back in the dark."

"He will not enter," says the Nameless.

His voice carries clearly in the stillness. Ruyan's head snaps round.

"I was told to see that you reach the first Dock alive," he says. "I was not told to go in. I take the distinction to be deliberate." He inclines his blank face toward the open door. "I will stand here. If anyone comes down the stair behind you, I will see that they do not reach you. That is all I am for."

"And if you are lying?" Ruyan says.

"Then you will have an excellent opportunity to use that sword," says the Nameless. There is the faintest trace of humor in it, and it makes Jian's skin crawl. "I would not blame you."

Nobody moves. Then Yue, of all of them, steps forward and bows, the correct bow, to a person of unknown rank.

"Thank you," she says.

The Nameless does not answer. But as she passes, Jian sees the gray head dip, a quarter inch, and the hands at its sides turn palm outward, a gesture so old and small that he almost misses it. It is how a man shows he is unarmed.

* * *

Dock Five is a room.

That is the first thing he notices. After the mountain of the Gate, after the vast cold green hall at the bottom of Azure Cloud, he had been braced for a cathedral. It is not. It is a low square chamber, perhaps twenty paces across, with a ceiling a hand's breadth above his head, built of the same dark green stone as the Gate wall. The air is dry and perfectly still. The dust lies on the floor in a skin as even as paint, and in the center of it, undisturbed, lies the pattern of a single set of footprints, going in, and none coming out.

There is a desk.

It is a plain wooden desk, with a stool, and on the desk a lamp of dull brass, a stack of paper held down by a stone, and a pen, uncapped. There is a cot against the wall. There is a cup. The cup has a ring of dried tea at the bottom.

He stops in the doorway. He cannot make himself step in.

"What is it?" says Yue.

"He lived here."

"Who?"

"The Operator." His throat is dry. "He sat at this desk. He drank from that cup. He walked in, and he did not walk out." He points to the footprints. "That is where he stood when the Gate took him."

Yue goes pale. She looks at the prints, at the cot, at the dust-skinned lamp. She has been quiet for a hundred and sixty days, and now, standing in the low green light of a room that has not breathed in six hundred years, she makes a small sound like a child.

"Oh," she says. "Oh, it is so lonely."

Pebble lays her ears flat.

"No," says the little beast. "It is not lonely. It is waiting."

* * *

Ruyan does not come in.

She stands in the doorway, with the lantern held a little behind her, and her toes exactly on the line where the stone changes from the rough brick of the stair to the smooth dark green of the chamber. She has not been told that she cannot cross. She simply does not. Her face in the light is hard and pale and puzzled.

"Priests' tales say that anyone who enters the sleeping lamp's room goes blind," she says. "Or mad. Or both."

"Do you believe it?"

"No." Her mouth is dry. "But I find I do not want to test it." She looks past Jian at the desk, at the dull brass lamp and the cup with its ring of tea, and her expression changes. "Somebody lived here."

"Yes."

"Alone."

"For six years."

"Then he was braver than I am." She says it quite simply, a trader stating a price. "I have a hundred and ten people on my payroll, and I count them every night to be sure they are alive. I could not do six years with a cup." She shifts the lantern. "Do you know what the worst thing is? It is neat. A man who knew he would die did not leave a mess. He washed the cup."

Jian looks at the cup. She is right. It has been rinsed, and set upside down on its saucer, in the way of someone who intended to come back.

"I will wait at the top with my guards," says Ruyan, after a moment. "If you are not out by dawn, I come down with a battering ram and the priests' blessing." She hesitates. "Lin Jian. If this room is what I think it is, then there are more of them."

"Yes. Four more, at least."

"And you will go to every one."

"If I can."

She nods slowly. "Then do not die in the first." The lantern swings, and her face is gone into shadow, and her boots ring away up the stair. Behind her, the corridor falls silent, and only Yue's quick breathing and the faint tick of Pebble's claws on the stone remain.

The Dock does not wake.

He lays his palm on the wall by the desk, the place where the stone is smoothest, and reaches for it. Nothing. He tries again. Nothing. The long, low hum he has felt since the city is stronger here, a single deep tone that fills the room, but it is not an answer. It is a held breath.

Eight. He has been earning two a night on the road, and spending four per step when he had to; Pebble has called out a dozen seams and he has walked through four. He has not been able to bank more than eight at a time. Twenty-two short.

"It needs thirty," he says.

"Can the Door pay?" asks Yue.

"The Door is not a source."

"Is it not?" She has come up beside him, quiet as a cat, and put her hand over his on the wall. Her fingers are cold. "Pebble says the Door is the same kind of thing as the Dock. A door in the soul. A door in the stone. If one is a copy of the other, then perhaps the stone will take what the soul gives."

He looks at her. "That is a guess."

"It is." She does not take her hand away. "But it is my guess, and you brought me here for my guesses."

He closes his eyes.

The hum in his breastbone is very quiet. He lets it widen, the way he did at the ford, and feels the cold flat plane of seams open under his ribs. He pushes against it. Not with his strength; with his attention. He thinks, Wake.

For a moment, nothing. Then, with a soft click like a latch giving way, something takes hold of him by the root of the spine and pulls.

* * *

It does not hurt, exactly. It feels like blood being drawn into a vial. A slow, deep, smooth withdrawal, from somewhere behind the sternum, through the arm, through the palm, into the stone. He sees a thin line of white light flow along the wall from his hand to the floor, and across the floor to the desk, and up the leg of the desk to the lamp. He hears Yue gasp.

The lamp lights.

It is not a flame. It is a clean small ball of pale gold, hovering above the wick, steady as a star. It gives off no heat. Every grain of dust in the room turns visible, hanging in the air like pollen, and on the desk, the stack of paper under its stone begins very faintly to glow.

His knees go. Yue catches him. For a minute he sees nothing, only white, and then the room swims back, and the hum has stopped, and the Dock is awake.

```
Paid: Seal -6% (now 69%)

for a sister site. It cannot pay twice.
Reading: Operator log available.
```

"Six percent," he says hoarsely.

"Is that bad?" Yue's voice is high and frightened.

"It is the Seal. It will mend." He wipes his mouth with the back of his hand; it comes away red. "It is a cost I can carry."

"Jian—"

"I am all right." He gets to his feet, unsteadily. "Look."

The paper on the desk is glowing. It is a stack of sheets, perhaps thirty, held down by a smooth black stone, and on top, in clear blue ink, in a small, cramped, tired hand that he knows as he knows his own face, a single line is written.

To whoever comes after.

* * *

He reads it standing, with Yue at his shoulder and Pebble on the desk between them.

To whoever comes after:

My name is Ethan Cole. I do not expect you to believe it, because I do not believe it myself. I have been here six years. I have made this log so that you do not have to start from the beginning, as I did.

I woke in a stone room with a scar on my left palm that I do not remember getting. I was told by a voice in my head that I was the fifth Operator of this Dock and that the four before me had left no record. I was told I had a task. I do not know what it is. I am writing it down so that I will know when I have done it.

Jian reads the line again.

the fifth Operator.

"Fifth," says Yue.

"Yes."

"But the Roll says all eight are the same man."

"They are." His mouth is dry. "That is what this is. A man who does not know he has done it before, writing to a man who does not know he will do it again."

He turns the page. And the next. Page after page of cramped blue handwriting, dated in a calendar he does not recognize, describing the Dock, the desert, the lamp. A pantry sealed with a seam. A recipe for a pill. A list of seven reagents. A diagram of the Gate, with the three stones drawn in the margin, and beside each a tiny neat note: LOCK. KEY. DOOR. A page that is simply a sketch of a woman's face, drawn in the ink and then crossed out, with the words underneath, I do not know who she is.

And at the bottom of the first page, below the signature, in a smaller hand, a note that has been added later.

He sees at once that it is different. The paper is the same, but the ink is wrong. It is a darker blue, richer, glossier, and its edges are crisp. It is not six hundred years old. It is barely a day old. It has been written by someone who stood where he is standing, a very short while ago, and walked out of the room, and left no footprints in the dust.

To Lin Jian, eighth Operator, age thirty-eight, who will arrive in the year the Keeper dies.

You have a sister who hears. Good. Keep her close.

Do not tell the others I knew.

—E.C.
